## What to Put on a Varsity Jacket: Names, Numbers, Logos & Patches

Once you've picked a style and color for your varsity jacket, the next question is usually the harder one: what actually goes on it, and where? Here's a practical guide to the standard placements — and when it's worth breaking from tradition.

## The Classic Layout

Traditional letterman jackets follow a fairly consistent placement pattern, and it's still the most common layout today:

**Chest, left side:** The main achievement letter or team/brand logo, usually the largest single element on the jacket. This is the focal point almost every retro or classic-style order builds around.

**Chest, right side:** An individual's name, embroidered directly onto the jacket — the detail that turns a group jacket into a personal one.

**Sleeve:** Smaller patches — graduation year, activity or sport icons, achievement patches, team captain markers. Sleeves are where most of the "extra" personalisation happens without crowding the chest.

**Back:** Reserved for bigger statements — a school or team name in large lettering, a mascot, or a full graphic design. Not every jacket needs back decoration, but it's the highest-impact placement if you want the jacket to make a statement from a distance.

## Names and Numbers

Individual names are almost always embroidered directly (not chenille) for a clean, legible finish, typically on the right chest. Numbers — common for sports teams — usually go on the sleeve or, less commonly, the back if the jacket doubles as a uniform piece. If you're ordering for a group, decide on font and placement once and apply it consistently across every jacket; mixing styles across a team order looks unintentional rather than customized.

## Logos and Patches

Brand or school logos typically take the main chest position if there's no achievement letter, or move to the sleeve if the chest is already occupied. For chenille, embroidered, or printed patches, the decoration method matters as much as the placement — chenille reads as classic and dimensional, embroidery is cleaner and more affordable at smaller sizes, and printed or DTF options work well for detailed, multi-color logos that would be difficult to embroider.

## Building Your Layout

If you're not sure how to lay out your specific design, a jacket designer lets you place names, numbers, patches, and logos directly on your jacket before ordering.

Getting placement right is part of every design proof sent before production starts.

content:
## Retro Varsity Jackets: Classic Style, Patches, and Color Ideas

Some varsity jacket orders aren't about following current trends — they're about leaning into the original collegiate look. Retro varsity jackets bring back the vintage color-blocking, wide ribbed trims, and chenille lettering that defined the style before it became a fashion staple. Here's how to build one that actually feels old-school rather than just "vintage-inspired" in name only.

## What Makes a Jacket Read as Retro

A handful of details separate a genuinely retro-feeling varsity jacket from a modern one:

**Bold color-blocking.** Classic letterman jackets leaned into strong, contrasting body-and-sleeve color pairs — think navy and white, maroon and cream, black and gold — rather than the more muted or single-tone builds common today.

**Wide ribbing.** Original varsity jackets typically used a wider rib knit at the collar, cuffs, and hem than a lot of modern builds. It's a small detail, but it's one of the fastest ways to make a jacket read as authentically vintage.

**Chenille lettering.** Large chenille letters and patches — the raised, textured lettering originally used for school achievement letters — are the single most recognizable retro design element. Modern jackets often use flatter embroidery instead; chenille is what gives a jacket that old-school, dimensional look.

**Classic placement.** A single large chenille letter centered on the chest, with smaller patches on the sleeve for year or activity, is the traditional layout — as opposed to the more graphic, asymmetric patch placements common on newer streetwear-influenced designs.

## Who Orders Retro Varsity Jackets

Retro builds are popular for alumni groups and reunions, throwback team merchandise, brands leaning into a nostalgic aesthetic, and anyone who wants a jacket that looks like it could have been made decades ago rather than this season. It's also a common choice for graduation jackets, where the classic look carries more sentimental weight than a modern silhouette.

## Building Yours

Start with the retro varsity jacket style, then pick your color-block pairing and chenille lettering. Retro-style orders are some of the most rewarding projects precisely because the details matter so much.

## Hooded Varsity Jackets: A Modern Letterman Style Guide

The classic letterman silhouette hasn't changed much in decades — but adding a hood is one of the more practical modern updates to the design. Here's what a hooded varsity jacket actually changes, and who it makes sense for.

## What a Hood Adds

A hooded varsity jacket keeps everything you'd expect from the classic build — ribbed collar, cuffs and hem, snap-button front, wool or leather construction — and adds a soft, lined hood at the neckline. It's a small change with a real practical benefit: more coverage on cold or wet days without giving up the varsity look entirely.

Visually, it also shifts the jacket slightly toward streetwear. The hood adds a more casual, modern silhouette that reads less like a school uniform and more like an everyday jacket — which is part of why hooded varsity jackets have become popular outside of traditional school and team orders.

## Who Hooded Varsity Jackets Work For

**Streetwear and fashion orders:** The hood is a distinctive design element that sets a jacket apart from the standard letterman silhouette — useful if you're building a brand piece meant to look current rather than purely traditional.

**Outdoor or exposed environments:** If your team or staff spend time outdoors — event staff, coaches on a sideline, outdoor clubs — the extra hood coverage is a genuine practical upgrade over a standard collar.

**Anyone who wants one jacket to do more:** A hood gives the jacket slightly more versatility across weather and settings than the classic open-collar build.

## What to Consider

A hood adds a small amount of bulk at the neckline and slightly changes how patches or embroidery near the collar are placed, so it's worth flagging in your design brief if you're planning detailed back or collar decoration. Otherwise, hooded varsity jackets take the same range of materials, colors, and customisation as the classic style.

## Cotton Twill Varsity Jackets: An Everyday Style Guide

Wool and leather aren't the only options for a custom varsity jacket. Cotton twill is a sturdy, wrinkle-resistant fabric that trades some of the heritage bulk of wool for a lighter, more casual, easier-to-maintain jacket. Here's when it makes sense.

## What Cotton Twill Brings to the Table

Cotton twill is a tightly woven, durable fabric — the same category of material used in work jackets and coach jackets — so it holds its shape well and resists wrinkling better than most alternatives. It's noticeably lighter than wool, which makes it more comfortable for all-season wear rather than being tied to cold weather specifically.

It's also low-maintenance. Cotton twill doesn't need the same care as leather sleeves or the dry-cleaning wool sometimes calls for, which matters if the jacket is going to see regular, everyday use rather than occasional wear.

## Where Cotton Twill Works Best

**Everyday and casual orders:** If the jacket needs to be worn often — not just for game days or special occasions — cotton twill's durability and easy care make it a practical choice.

**Warmer or mixed climates:** Cotton twill doesn't carry the insulation of wool, so it suits regions or seasons where a full wool-and-leather build would be too warm.

**Budget-conscious bulk orders:** Cotton twill is typically a more affordable option than leather-sleeve builds, which matters for large team or school orders where per-unit cost adds up quickly.

## What to Keep in Mind

Cotton twill won't give you the same premium, structured look as wool or leather — it reads as more casual, which is either exactly what you want or a reason to look at a different fabric depending on the occasion. It still takes embroidery and printed patches well, though very dense chenille work sits slightly differently on twill than on wool.

## Getting Started

Cotton twill is one of the most requested options for schools and brands ordering jackets meant for daily wear rather than occasional use.

title: Satin Varsity Jackets: Lightweight Style Guide

## Satin Varsity Jackets: A Lightweight Style Guide

Not every varsity jacket needs to be built for winter. Satin varsity jackets trade wool and leather for glossy, lightweight polyester satin — a completely different feel, and a completely different set of use cases. Here's what to know before you order one.

## What Makes Satin Different

Satin is smooth, glossy, and noticeably lighter than wool or leather. It's the same fabric traditionally used for souvenir jackets and baseball jackets, which is part of why satin varsity jackets have a slightly different visual identity than the classic collegiate wool-and-leather build — more fashion statement, less winter uniform.

Because it's lightweight, satin doesn't insulate the way wool does. That's a feature, not a flaw, depending on what you need the jacket for.

## Where Satin Works Best

**Mild climates and indoor events:** If your jacket needs to look sharp at an event, on stage, or somewhere temperature-controlled rather than keep you warm outdoors, satin is the more comfortable choice.

**Fashion and brand pieces:** The glossy finish photographs well and gives designs — especially embroidery and printed graphics — a bold, high-shine backdrop. Satin jackets are popular for music merch, streetwear drops, and statement pieces.

**Layering:** Because it's light, a satin jacket layers easily over hoodies or shirts without adding bulk, which wool and leather builds don't always allow.

## What to Consider Before Ordering

Satin doesn't hold chenille patches quite as securely as wool does — embroidery and printed graphics tend to be the better decoration choice on satin. It's also less durable under heavy daily wear than wool or leather, so it suits jackets that get worn for events and occasions more than a jacket that needs to survive a full sports season of practice.

Color-wise, satin takes bright, saturated tones especially well thanks to its sheen — if you want a jacket that pops in photos, this is the material to consider.

## Getting Started

Satin jackets work for everything from single fashion pieces to bulk brand orders.

title: All-Leather vs Wool-and-Leather Varsity Jackets
excerpt: The classic wool-and-leather build or a full all-leather jacket? Here's how the two premium varsity jacket styles actually compare in weight, cost, and look.
content:
## All-Leather vs Wool-and-Leather Varsity Jackets: Which Should You Order?

Two of the most requested varsity jacket builds look similar at a glance but feel and wear very differently: the classic wool and leather combination, and the all-leather build. Here's how to decide between them.

## Wool and Leather: The Classic Letterman Build

This is the original varsity jacket construction — a wool body paired with leather sleeves, usually in a contrasting color. It's the build most people picture when they think "letterman jacket": warm, structured, and instantly recognizable. Wool holds embroidery and chenille patches especially well, which is part of why it's remained the standard for school and team orders for decades.

Wool and leather works best for: schools, sports teams, alumni groups, and anyone who wants the traditional varsity look.

## All-Leather: The Premium, Modern Alternative

An all-leather varsity jacket keeps the same silhouette — ribbed collar, cuffs, and hem, snap-button front — but replaces the wool body with leather as well, so the whole jacket is one consistent material. The result is a heavier, more durable jacket with a bolder, more fashion-forward look. It's popular with streetwear brands and anyone ordering a jacket as a standalone fashion piece rather than a team uniform.

All-leather works best for: brand merchandise, streetwear drops, fashion-forward personal orders, and anyone who wants a jacket that reads as premium rather than collegiate.

## Practical Differences to Weigh

**Weight and warmth:** Wool and leather is generally lighter and more breathable across the body, since only the sleeves carry the heavier leather. An all-leather jacket is heavier overall — great for cooler climates, less ideal if you need something to layer easily.

**Cost:** All-leather typically costs more than wool and leather, since leather is the more expensive material and there's more of it in the jacket.

**Look:** Wool and leather gives you a two-tone contrast by default. All-leather can be ordered in a single color for a sleeker, more uniform look, or still contrast the sleeve tone against the body.

**Customisation:** Both builds take embroidery, chenille patches, names, and numbers well, though wool has a very slightly softer surface for chenille work.

## Making the Call

If you're outfitting a school or team and want the classic look people expect, wool and leather is the safer, more traditional choice. If you're building a brand, a limited drop, or want something that feels more premium and less "team uniform," all-leather is worth the extra cost.

title: Varsity Jacket vs Letterman Jacket: What's the Difference?
excerpt: Varsity jacket or letterman jacket — are they actually different? Here's the real story behind both terms, and what actually matters when you're ordering one.
content:
## Varsity Jacket vs Letterman Jacket: What's the Difference?

If you've been shopping for a custom jacket, you've probably seen "varsity jacket" and "letterman jacket" used for what looks like the exact same garment — wool body, leather sleeves, ribbed trims, chenille letters on the chest. So is there actually a difference? Here's the honest answer.

## Same Jacket, Different Origin Story

"Letterman jacket" comes from American high schools, where the jacket was awarded to students who earned a varsity "letter" — the school's initial, in chenille, on the chest — for achievement in sports, academics, or other activities. The jacket itself became known by the letter it carried.

"Varsity jacket" refers to the same silhouette, but the word "varsity" points to the level of the team (the top, or "varsity," level of a school's sports program) rather than the award itself. Over time, as the jacket moved beyond schools into general fashion, "varsity jacket" became the more common term — you'll see it used for streetwear, brand merchandise, and team apparel just as often as school lettering.

## Is There Any Real Difference Today?

In practice, no — the two terms describe the same jacket: a wool or leather body, contrast leather or wool sleeves, ribbed collar, cuffs and hem, and a snap-button closure, customizable with patches, embroidery, names, and numbers. "Letterman jacket" leans slightly more toward the school-and-achievement context, while "varsity jacket" is used more broadly for fashion, team, and brand orders. Neither term is more "correct" — it's regional and contextual, with "varsity jacket" the dominant term in the UK and much of Europe.

## What This Means When You're Ordering

Don't worry about which word to use when you're getting a quote — any custom jacket supplier worth using will recognize both terms as the same product. What actually matters is the construction: body material, sleeve material, patch and embroidery placement, and fit.

If you're ordering for a school, the classic wool and leather build is the most traditional "letterman" look. If you want something with more of a fashion edge, styles like all-leather or retro lean further into varsity-as-streetwear territory.

title: How to Choose Between Leather and Coated Bomber Jackets
excerpt: Leather or coated bomber jacket — which should you order? Compare durability, weight, weather resistance, and cost to pick the right build.
content:
## How to Choose Between Leather and Coated Bomber Jackets

Bomber jackets come in two very different material families — genuine or suede leather, and coated fabrics like nylon twill or softshell. They share the same silhouette, but wear, look, and feel completely differently. Here's how to choose.

## Leather Bombers: Classic, Durable, Premium

A leather bomber — usually cowhide or sheep leather — is the traditional choice. It has a natural texture, structured drape, and ages well with wear, developing a broken-in look that coated fabrics can't replicate. Sheep leather in particular is lighter and softer than cowhide, giving a cleaner, more flexible finish.

Leather works best for: fashion pieces, brand merchandise, and anyone who wants a jacket that looks and feels premium from day one and improves with age.

The trade-off: leather costs more, weighs more, and needs occasional conditioning to stay supple.

## Coated Bombers: Lightweight, Practical, Weather-Ready

A coated bomber — typically nylon twill or softshell — trades leather's heft for a lighter, more weather-resistant jacket. Nylon twill is water-resistant and holds up well to daily wear, while softshell adds a bit more warmth and flexibility for outdoor use. Both take embroidery and printed logos cleanly, and neither requires the maintenance leather does.

Coated fabrics work best for: bulk team orders, corporate uniforms, and anyone who needs a practical, easy-care jacket rather than a fashion statement piece.

## Practical Differences

**Weight:** Coated fabrics are noticeably lighter than leather, which matters for jackets worn all day.

**Weather resistance:** Nylon and softshell handle light rain and wind better than untreated leather.

**Cost:** Leather bombers cost more — both the material itself and the extra care they need.

**Customisation:** Both take embroidery well; coated fabrics are usually the better base for large printed logos since leather needs specific techniques (debossing, leather patches) rather than direct printing.

## Making the Call

If the jacket is a personal or brand piece meant to be worn for years, leather is worth the investment. If you're ordering for a team, staff, or event where practicality and budget matter more than premium feel, a coated bomber is the smarter choice.

title: The Difference Between a $50 Jacket and a $150 Jacket: What You're Actually Paying For
excerpt: Why does one custom jacket cost $50 and another $150? It's not just the brand name. Here's an honest breakdown of exactly what changes at different price points.
content:
## The Difference Between a $50 Jacket and a $150 Jacket: What You're Actually Paying For

One of the most common questions from first-time bulk buyers is some version of: why is there such a big price difference between suppliers? You can find a custom varsity jacket for $45 per unit and another that costs $150. They might look similar in a product photo. So what are you actually getting for the extra money?

This is a genuinely important question — because the answer affects whether you end up with jackets that last three seasons or jackets that go in the bin after one. Here's an honest breakdown of what changes at different price points.

### Fabric Quality: Where the Biggest Difference Lives

The single biggest cost driver in a custom jacket is the fabric. And this is where the most significant quality differences show up.

At the lower price point, you'll typically find: thin wool blends (or fabrics marketed as wool that contain very little actual wool), lightweight faux leather with a thin PU coating that cracks and peels within a season or two, synthetic lining that feels plasticky against the skin, and lightweight ribbing on cuffs and collar that loses its elasticity quickly.

At the higher price point, you get: heavier weight wool or wool-blend fabric with a substantially better hand feel, thicker faux leather or genuine leather on the sleeves with a coating that holds up to repeated wear, a smoother, more comfortable lining, and ribbed trims that retain their shape and elasticity over multiple seasons.

The difference is immediately obvious when you hold both jackets. One feels solid and substantial. The other feels like it's pretending to be a jacket.

### Construction: How the Jacket Is Put Together

Fabric quality is only part of the story. The construction — how the jacket is sewn together — determines how long it lasts under real-world use.

Lower price point jackets often use fewer stitches per seam, cheaper thread that fades and weakens over time, lightweight snap buttons or zips that fail after moderate use, and seam finishing that frays with washing. The jackets can look fine when new, but they degrade noticeably after six to twelve months of regular use.

Higher quality jackets use reinforced seams at stress points (shoulders, sleeve joins, pocket openings), durable hardware that's been tested for repeated use, consistent stitching density throughout, and finished seams that don't fray in the wash.

### Customisation Quality: The Embroidery and Patches

This is where many buyers are caught off guard. A low price doesn't just mean cheaper fabric — it often means lower quality embroidery, thinner chenille patches, less precise placement, and thread colours that fade significantly after washing.

Premium custom jackets use higher stitch count embroidery that creates a denser, more vibrant finish. Chenille patches use quality wool chenille rather than synthetic alternatives. Patch placement is consistent across all units in a batch. Thread colours are matched to specification and remain colour-fast through multiple washes.

If the jacket is meant to represent your brand, team, or school — the quality of the embellishment matters just as much as the fabric.

### Longevity: The Real Cost Calculation

Here's the calculation that many buyers miss. A $50 jacket that lasts one season and then needs to be replaced costs more over two years than an $100 jacket that lasts four seasons. The apparent savings aren't savings at all — they're a deferred cost.

For one-off event jackets that will be worn occasionally, a lower price point may be entirely appropriate. For team uniforms, graduation keepsakes, or brand merchandise that people are expected to wear regularly and keep for years — the investment in quality pays for itself.

### What to Expect Across Price Points

A practical, decent-quality jacket for a one-day event at a competitive price is a reasonable option, and so is a premium, long-lasting jacket meant to be worn for years — the right choice depends on what you actually need.

What matters most is transparency: you should know exactly what fabric and construction you're getting at a given price, so you can make a genuinely informed decision rather than being sold low-quality materials passed off as premium.

title: Why Jacket Fit Matters More Than You Think — and How to Get It Right
excerpt: The design on your custom jacket can be perfect, but if the fit is wrong, the jacket looks wrong. Here's why fit is the most underrated element of a group jacket order.
content:
## Why Jacket Fit Matters More Than You Think — and How to Get It Right

In a group jacket order, it's easy to focus on the things that feel most visible: the colours, the logo, the patches, the personalisation. But the element that has the single biggest impact on how the jacket actually looks on a person? Fit. And it's the one that gets the least attention until something goes wrong.

A jacket with a perfect design but a bad fit looks cheap. A simple jacket with a perfect fit looks premium. Here's why this matters so much — and how to get it right for every person in your order.

## Why Fit Makes or Breaks the Jacket

Clothes communicate two things simultaneously: the design, and how the person wearing them feels about themselves. A well-fitting jacket communicates confidence. It sits correctly at the shoulder, doesn't pull across the chest, allows comfortable arm movement, and falls at the right length on the torso. When someone puts it on and it fits properly, they stand differently. They wear it more.

A poorly fitting jacket does the opposite. Shoulders that are too wide make the person look smaller. A chest that's too tight looks uncomfortable and strains seams. A hem that's too long makes the jacket look borrowed. These are the things that make people leave the jacket in the cupboard instead of wearing it.

For group orders, this is amplified. If most of the team's jackets fit well but a handful don't, those individuals feel singled out — even if no one mentions it. The goal of a team jacket is unity and pride, and a poor fit undermines both.

## The Most Common Fit Mistakes in Group Orders

The most common error is people self-reporting sizes from another brand without accounting for sizing differences. Brand A's large is not always Brand B's large. Without a size guide specific to the jacket being ordered, people guess — and guesses are often wrong.

The second most common error is people sizing down because they don't want to appear to be a larger size. The result is a jacket that's too tight across the shoulders or chest, pulls when they move, and looks strained.

The third is not accounting for layering. A jacket worn directly over a t-shirt in summer may need to be a size larger than expected if it's going to be worn over a thick jumper or hoodie in winter.

## How to Measure Correctly for a Custom Jacket

The most important measurement for a jacket is chest circumference. Measure around the fullest part of the chest, keeping the tape horizontal and adding 2-4 inches of ease for a regular fit (more for an oversized style). This measurement, compared against the supplier's size chart, gives you the correct size regardless of what size the person normally buys in other brands.

For teams, the most practical approach is to provide a size chart alongside your size collection form. Ask people to measure their chest and match it to the chart rather than selecting a size by letter. This one step alone dramatically reduces the number of sizing issues in a group order.

## Should You Size Up or Down When In Between?

For structured jackets — varsity, bombers, anything with a defined shoulder seam — size up when in between. A jacket that's slightly large can be worn comfortably and still looks intentional. A jacket that's slightly small looks tight and feels restrictive.

For more relaxed silhouettes — coach jackets, fleeces, puffer jackets — either size works, but sizing true-to-measurement gives the cleanest result.

## Getting Fit Right

A detailed size guide for the specific jacket style being ordered removes the guesswork — sizing varies between jacket constructions, and the exact chest-to-size conversion should be given upfront rather than left to guesswork.

title: How Our Quality Check Works Before Your Order Ships
excerpt: Wondering what happens to your custom jacket order before it leaves the facility? Here's a transparent look at exactly how orders are checked for quality, accuracy, and consistency before shipping.
content:
## How Our Quality Check Works Before Your Order Ships

When you place a custom jacket order, you're trusting that what arrives matches what you approved. That's not something to take lightly. Every order goes through a structured quality check process before it leaves the facility — and here's exactly what that looks like.

## Step 1: Design Accuracy Check

The first thing checked is whether every jacket in the order matches the approved design proof. This means verifying the colours of the body and sleeves against the agreed specification, confirming that every logo, patch, and embroidery placement is in the correct position, checking that any personalisation (individual names, numbers, or custom text) matches the submitted name list exactly, and confirming that font, thread colour, and stitch density are consistent across all units.

This is done unit by unit, not as a batch check. Each jacket is individually compared against the proof and the order specification.

## Step 2: Construction and Materials Inspection

Once design accuracy is confirmed, each jacket is inspected for construction quality. This includes the stitching on seams, cuffs, and collar for any loose threads, skipped stitches, or inconsistencies; snap buttons and zip closures to confirm they open and close correctly; the sleeve attachment points, which carry the most stress in a varsity jacket; and the lining attachment and any interior details for cleanliness and consistency.

For jackets with genuine leather sleeves, the leather is also inspected for any surface marks, uneven colouring, or application issues that occurred during manufacturing.

## Step 3: Size Verification

Before packing, each jacket is checked against its size label to confirm it matches the actual garment measurements. This step catches any mislabelling that can occur during production — particularly important in large orders where sizes vary significantly across the batch.

Packed sizes are then cross-referenced against the original size breakdown submitted with the order to confirm the quantities are correct before the box is sealed.

## Step 4: Final Presentation Check

Jackets are folded or hung according to style (structured jackets are typically hung on internal cardboard forms to maintain shape during transit). The presentation layer — how the jacket looks when it comes out of the packaging — matters too, especially for premium or gifted orders.

Any jacket that doesn't meet the standard at this stage is pulled out of the batch and either corrected before shipping or replaced.

## What Happens If Something Gets Through

Despite thorough checks, occasionally an issue reaches a customer — it's rare, but honest suppliers acknowledge it can happen. If you receive a jacket with a quality issue, contact support within 7 days of delivery with photographs of the problem for assessment and resolution — replacement, correction, or an appropriate alternative.

## Why This Matters for Bulk Orders

For group orders of 20, 50, or 200+ jackets, a quality issue that slips through creates a much bigger problem than it would for a single garment. One wrong name, one misaligned patch, one incorrect size label — multiplied across a large order — creates a significant disruption for the person managing the distribution.

The quality check process is specifically designed for bulk custom orders where consistency across the batch is just as important as the quality of any individual unit.

title: What to Do If Your Jacket Patch Starts to Peel or Loosen
excerpt: A peeling or loosening jacket patch doesn't always mean the jacket is ruined. In most cases, it can be fixed cleanly and permanently. Here's what to do — and what to avoid.
content:
## What to Do If Your Jacket Patch Starts to Peel or Loosen

A peeling patch is one of the most frustrating things that can happen to a custom jacket. You've invested in something that was supposed to last, and now the corner of your chenille letter or embroidered badge is starting to lift. Before you write it off, the good news is: in most cases, this is completely fixable. Here's how.

### First, Understand Why It's Happening

Not all patches are applied the same way, and the cause of peeling affects the fix. The most common reasons a patch starts to lift are:

#### Heat damage
Patches applied with heat-activated adhesive can begin to lift if the jacket has been washed on too high a temperature or tumble dried. The adhesive bond breaks down with repeated heat exposure.

#### Edge wear
The edges of a patch — particularly corners — are the first to lift because they experience the most stress from movement and wear. Even well-applied patches can start to lift at the edges after extended heavy use.

#### Incorrect application
If a patch wasn't applied with sufficient pressure, heat, or time during the original application, the adhesive bond was never fully set and will fail sooner than expected.

#### Moisture
Repeated washing or prolonged dampness can weaken both the adhesive and the backing of a patch over time.

### What Not to Do

Before the fix, here's what to avoid. Don't pull the patch further off — this tears the fibres of the jacket body fabric underneath and makes repair much harder. Don't apply standard craft glue or super glue — these are too rigid when dry and will cause the patch to crack and look worse. Don't iron directly onto the patch without a protective cloth — this can melt synthetic fibres in the patch and cause irreversible damage.

### Fix Option 1: Fabric Bond Adhesive (For Small Lifts)

If it's just a corner or edge that's lifting and the rest of the patch is secure, a fabric bond adhesive (also called fabric glue or hem tape) is the easiest fix. Apply a small amount under the lifting edge, press firmly and hold for 30-60 seconds, then place a heavy book or flat weight on top while it sets (usually 10-15 minutes). Most fabric adhesives are wash-resistant when fully cured, so they'll hold through subsequent cleaning.

### Fix Option 2: Re-Ironing (For Heat-Applied Patches)

If your patch was originally applied with heat-activated adhesive, re-ironing can re-activate the bond. Place a thin cotton cloth between the iron and the patch to protect the fabric, and apply firm pressure with a medium-hot iron for 15-20 seconds. Do not move the iron while pressing. The heat reactivates the adhesive and the pressure resets the bond. Let it cool flat before moving the jacket.

### Fix Option 3: Stitch It Down (Permanent Solution)

If the patch keeps lifting after adhesive fixes, the most reliable long-term solution is to have it stitched down around the perimeter. A local tailor or seamstress can do this in minutes. Stitching around the edge not only secures the patch permanently but also looks intentional and adds a premium, professional finish.

### When to Contact Your Jacket Supplier

If the patch starts peeling within a few weeks of receiving a new jacket — before any washing or heavy use — that's a quality issue that your supplier should address. Document it with photographs (close-up of the lifting area, plus a wider shot showing the full jacket) and get in touch promptly.

title: How to Store Your Jacket Between Seasons Without Damaging It
excerpt: You've invested in a quality custom jacket — the last thing you want is to pull it out next season and find it misshapen, mouldy, or faded. Here's exactly how to store it properly.
content:
## How to Store Your Jacket Between Seasons Without Damaging It

You spent good money on a quality custom jacket. It looks great, it fits well, and your team loves it. Then the season ends, it goes into storage — and six months later, you pull it out to find the wool has pilled, the leather sleeves have cracked, or there's a musty smell that wasn't there before.

Proper storage takes ten minutes. It saves you from replacing a jacket that should have lasted years. Here's exactly what to do.

### Clean It Before You Store It

This is the step most people skip, and it's the most important one. Never store a dirty jacket. Sweat, body oils, food residue, and invisible stains all break down fabric over time — and they attract moths and other insects that can cause permanent damage.

For wool-bodied jackets: dry clean or spot clean before storage. Do not machine wash a wool varsity jacket. For faux leather sleeves: wipe down with a damp cloth and a mild soap solution, then let it dry completely before storing. For genuine leather sleeves: apply a small amount of leather conditioner before storage. This keeps the leather supple and prevents cracking during long periods without wear.

Always make sure the jacket is completely dry before it goes into storage. Even slight dampness can cause mould to develop in an enclosed space.

### Use a Proper Hanger — Not a Wire One

A wire dry-cleaning hanger will distort the shoulder seams of a jacket over time. Use a wide, padded hanger that supports the full width of the shoulders. This maintains the jacket's shape during storage and prevents those frustrating shoulder bumps that are almost impossible to remove.

### Store It in a Breathable Garment Bag

Plastic garment bags trap moisture and can cause condensation, which leads to mould and mildew. Use a breathable cotton or non-woven fabric garment bag instead. This allows air to circulate around the jacket while keeping dust and insects out.

Avoid storing jackets in sealed plastic boxes or vacuum storage bags — these are designed for fabrics that don't need to breathe, and they can damage structured garments like jackets.

### Choose the Right Storage Location

Where you store the jacket matters as much as how. Avoid: attics (temperature extremes and humidity damage both wool and leather), basements (damp environments accelerate mould), direct sunlight (fades colour rapidly), and areas near radiators or heating vents (dry heat cracks leather and dries out wool).

The ideal storage location is a cool, dry, dark space with stable temperature — a bedroom wardrobe or a dedicated coat cupboard is usually perfect.

### Add Cedar Blocks or Lavender Sachets

Both cedar and lavender are natural moth deterrents. Place a cedar block or a small lavender sachet inside the garment bag with your jacket. Replace cedar blocks annually as they lose effectiveness over time. This simple step protects your jacket from one of the most common causes of wool garment damage during storage.

### Check It Periodically

If the jacket is in storage for more than three months, take it out once to air it and check for any issues. A quick inspection every few months allows you to catch any problems — a developing spot, a moth issue, unexpected dampness — before they become irreversible.

### Bringing It Back Out

When the season comes around again, take the jacket out a few days early. Let it air at room temperature for 24 hours before wearing it. For leather sleeves that feel slightly stiff, a small amount of leather conditioner worked in gently will restore suppleness. For wool that has any minor creasing, steaming (not ironing directly) will relax the fibres without damaging the fabric.

Wool-bodied and leather-sleeve styles each need slightly different care, so check which fabric your jacket uses before storing it.

title: How to Use Custom Jackets as Event Merchandise People Actually Keep

content:
## How to Use Custom Jackets as Event Merchandise People Actually Keep

Most event merchandise has a short shelf life. Branded tote bags, mugs, pens — people take them home, use them briefly, and then they disappear. The brand impression lasts a few weeks at best.

A custom jacket is different. When it's designed well, it becomes something people actively want to wear — which means your brand stays visible for months or years after the event ends. Here's how to make it work.

## Make It Look Good, Not Just Branded

The fundamental mistake with branded merchandise is putting the brand before the product. A jacket covered in oversized logos and corporate colours looks like corporate merchandise — and people don't wear corporate merchandise voluntarily.

The best event jackets are ones where the design is genuinely attractive, with the brand integrated tastefully rather than aggressively. A small embroidered logo on the chest. An event name and year on the back in a clean, confident font. Colours chosen for aesthetic appeal, not just brand compliance.

When the jacket looks good, people wear it. When they wear it, your brand travels with them.

## Create Exclusivity Around the Jacket

If everyone gets a jacket at a mass-market event, it feels like a giveaway. If only a select group gets one — VIP attendees, speakers, volunteers, key sponsors — the jacket becomes a marker of status and belonging.

Consider positioning the jacket as something earned or given to a select group. The scarcity makes it more desirable and more likely to be worn proudly rather than thrown in a drawer.

## Choose the Right Product Tier

Not all branded jackets are created equal. A thin, low-quality jacket in a generic style will communicate exactly the opposite of what you intend. Investing in a quality product sends a message that the brand or event takes quality seriously.

For events where the jacket is a key brand touch-point, a quality varsity jacket, premium bomber, or a well-made fleece is worth the extra cost per unit. The perceived value to the recipient is disproportionately higher than the cost difference.

## Include Personalisation Where Possible

A jacket with an attendee's name on it is a jacket they will almost certainly keep. Personalisation transforms merchandise from a generic branded item into something personal. If your event has a fixed attendee list, use it — order individual names on the chest or sleeve for every recipient.

For events where personalisation isn't logistically feasible, an event-specific design that's clearly tied to the moment (event name, year, location) still creates a keepsake quality that generic merchandise lacks.

## Plan the Jacket as Part of the Event Experience

Don't distribute jackets as an afterthought. Make the jacket reveal part of the event itself — a moment where everyone receives their jacket at the same time, ideally early in the event so they wear it throughout the day and photographs capture the brand naturally.

A varsity jacket or bomber jacket both work well as premium merch, with individual names added cleanly via embroidery.

## Corporate Away Day Uniforms: Why a Custom Jacket Beats a Polo Every Time

The branded polo shirt is the default corporate away day uniform. It's safe, it's relatively cheap, and it does the job of making a group look vaguely unified. But it rarely makes anyone feel good, and it almost never gets worn again after the event. It goes in the back of a wardrobe or, more likely, the charity bag.

A custom jacket is different. Here's why it consistently outperforms the polo for corporate away days — and why the extra investment is usually justified.

## A Jacket Gets Worn Again

The single most important difference is wearability. A branded polo shirt is recognisably a work item — it signals "corporate function" in a way that limits when people will wear it. A well-designed custom jacket, on the other hand, is something people might actually wear on a weekend, during a commute, or at a casual social event. That means your brand travels beyond the away day itself, into the daily lives of your team.

Every time a team member wears the jacket outside of work, they're a walking advert for your brand. The polo doesn't do that.

## It Communicates Investment in Your Team

Corporate events are as much about team morale as they are about the content of the day. A branded jacket communicates that the company invested in something of quality — not just the cheapest branded item they could order from a catalogue. That's a message that lands differently than a polo shirt.

Teams that feel valued perform better and retain higher employee satisfaction. The jacket is a tangible expression of that value.

## It Works Outdoors

Away days are often partially or fully outdoors — activity days, team-building exercises, site visits, outdoor workshops. A polo shirt is hopelessly impractical in cold or wet weather. A jacket isn't. Your team stays warm, the event goes ahead regardless of weather, and nobody spends the afternoon with their arms crossed trying to stay warm.

For outdoor away days specifically, a mid-layer jacket or a water-resistant coach jacket is significantly more practical than any top without an outer layer.

## It's a Better Canvas for Branding

Jackets have more surface area for branding than polo shirts — back panels, chest logos, sleeve detailing. The design possibilities are substantially wider. A jacket can carry a large back print or embroidered crest that a polo simply can't accommodate at the same visual impact.

## What to Order for a Corporate Away Day

For most corporate away days, a bomber jacket, coach jacket, or fleece is the right call. Something light enough to be comfortable during activities, but substantial enough to handle variable outdoor weather. Simple embroidery on the left chest with the company logo is classic and professional. Individual names on the chest add a personal touch that teams appreciate.

## Why Sports Teams Are Ordering Custom Jackets for Award Nights & Banquets

The end-of-season awards night is a tradition for sports teams of all levels. Whether it's a grassroots football club, a university rowing team, or a professional youth academy, the awards banquet marks the end of a chapter and celebrates the people who made it happen.

For years, the standard format was trophies, plaques, and certificates. But increasingly, custom jackets are becoming the award item of choice — and for good reason.

## A Jacket Is Something They'll Actually Keep

Trophies gather dust. Certificates go in a drawer. A well-made custom jacket gets worn. It's a wearable trophy that travels with the recipient and continues to represent the team long after the season ends. That's genuine, ongoing value — not just a moment of recognition that fades by Monday morning.

## It Creates a Sense of Belonging

When the whole squad receives a custom jacket at the end of the year, it creates a shared moment. Everyone is recognised equally. The jacket becomes a symbol of having been part of this specific team, in this specific season. For many players, particularly younger ones, that sense of belonging and recognition is more meaningful than any individual award.

## They Double as Team Uniforms for the Night

A custom jacket also solves the perennial problem of what team members wear to an awards night. When everyone arrives in the same jacket, the event feels more cohesive and photogenic. The team looks like a team — not just a group of individuals at a venue.

## Premium Jackets Work as Awards for Standout Players

Some clubs use custom jackets strategically — the whole team receives a standard jacket, while award recipients (Player of the Year, Top Scorer, Most Improved) receive a premium version with additional personalisation: a specific patch, a gold thread version of their name, or a special edition colourway. This creates a tiered recognition system within the same product family.

## What to Order for an Awards Night

For a team awards night, varsity jackets are the most popular choice. The classic wool-and-leather construction feels premium enough to make the occasion special. Individual names on the chest are almost always included — it's what transforms the jacket from a generic team item into a personal memento.

Key design elements for an award night jacket: team name and season year on the back, individual name on the chest, team colours, and any achievement patches for specific recipients.

## Timeline for Awards Night Orders

Custom jackets for an end-of-season event should be ordered 6-8 weeks before the date. This allows time for design approval, name collection, production, and delivery. Don't wait until the last few weeks of the season — that's when orders stack up and lead times extend.

content:
## Custom Graduation Jackets: How Schools Are Replacing Gowns With Lettermans

Graduation gowns have tradition behind them. But for many schools, colleges, and sixth forms, the custom varsity jacket has emerged as a compelling alternative — or companion — to the traditional cap-and-gown format. Here's why the trend is growing, and what you need to know if you're considering it for your graduating class.

## Why the Shift Is Happening

The traditional graduation gown is often hired, not owned. After the ceremony, it goes back. Students are left with a photo and a certificate — but nothing physical to commemorate the experience. A custom varsity jacket changes that. It's something students actually keep, wear, and value long after the ceremony.

Beyond the sentimental value, a jacket with the school name, graduating year, and individual name embroidered is a wearable memory that can't be replicated by a hired gown. It's personal in a way that mass-produced gowns simply aren't.

## What Makes a Good Graduation Jacket?

The best graduation jackets balance school identity with individual personalisation. Here's what most schools include:

**School name and crest on the back:** Usually the centrepiece of the design. A well-executed crest or logo on the back panel creates a recognisable, distinctive piece that represents the institution properly.

**Year of graduation on the front chest:** A classic detail that marks the milestone clearly — typically in chenille or embroidery.

**Individual name on the chest or sleeve:** What transforms a group jacket into a personal keepsake. Names are typically embroidered on the right chest in a complementary font.

**School colours:** The body and sleeve colours should reflect the school's official palette. This is where it matters to work with a supplier who can accurately match Pantone references.

## Planning a School-Wide Graduation Jacket Order

The logistics of a school jacket order are similar to any group order — but with a few specific considerations:

**Lead time:** Graduation dates are fixed. Start the jacket order process at least 8-10 weeks before graduation to allow for design approval, individual name collection, and production. Spring graduation orders placed in January or February are ideal.

**Name and personalisation collection:** Each student's name needs to be confirmed before production. Use a Google Form or spreadsheet to collect names, spellings, and any other personalisation details. Include a deadline and communicate that late submissions may miss the batch.

**Budget:** School budgets vary. Custom graduation jackets are typically priced between $45-$90 per unit depending on fabric, sleeve material, and customisation complexity. For year group orders of 50+ units, bulk pricing significantly reduces the per-unit cost.

## The Seasonal Opportunity

If you're a school or college coordinator reading this in autumn or winter, now is the right time to start planning. Spring graduations in May and June are the busiest period for custom jacket orders, and schools that plan early get the best results.

title: How to Order Staff Jackets for a Large Outdoor Event (Without the Stress)
excerpt: Ordering staff jackets for a large outdoor event? From lead times to size collection to delivery logistics, here's how to get it right the first time.
content:
## How to Order Staff Jackets for a Large Outdoor Event (Without the Stress)

If you're running a large outdoor event — a festival, a sporting event, a community fair, a corporate conference — your staff jackets serve two purposes. They identify your team clearly in a busy environment, and they represent your event's brand to everyone who sees them.

Getting the order right is important. Getting it right on time is critical. Here's how to manage the process without the last-minute stress.

## Start Earlier Than You Think You Need To

The most common mistake with event jackets is starting the process too late. Custom jackets typically take 3-6 weeks from approved design to delivery. For large events with complex requirements — multiple roles, different colourways, or very high volumes — the timeline can stretch further.

As a rule of thumb, start your jacket order process 8 weeks before the event. This gives you time for design iteration, size collection, production, and delivery — with a buffer for any delays.

## Define Your Requirements Before You Start

Before contacting a supplier, have answers to these questions: How many staff members need jackets? Are there different roles that need to be visually distinct (e.g., security, volunteers, event management)? What's the weather likely to be? What logo and branding elements are required?

Knowing the answers in advance will dramatically speed up the quoting and design process.

## Choose the Right Jacket for Outdoor Use

For outdoor events, practicality matters as much as appearance. Consider: weather resistance (will it be cold? wet?), visibility in crowded environments, weight and comfort for staff wearing them for 8-12 hour shifts, and whether the jacket needs to accommodate layers underneath.

Coach jackets, bomber jackets, and puffer vests are all popular for event use. If the weather is unpredictable, a lightweight jacket with some water resistance is usually the smart call.

## Collect Sizes With a Deadline

Use a Google Form or shared spreadsheet to collect sizes. Give your team a firm deadline and make it clear that anyone who doesn't respond will receive a medium (or whatever size you designate as the default). This prevents the endless chasing that delays so many orders.

For large teams, assign someone at each department or team level to collect sizes from their group and report back to the central coordinator.

## Plan for Last-Minute Staff Additions

Event staffing changes right up to the last day. Plan for this by ordering 5-10% more jackets than you think you need in the most common sizes. It's far less stressful to have a handful of spare jackets than to have new staff turn up on event day without one.

## Confirm Delivery in Advance

Confirm the delivery address, window, and contact name well in advance. For very large orders, ask your supplier whether they can stagger delivery or provide jackets pre-sorted by size or role. This saves significant time on distribution day.

For outdoor shifts, coach jackets and puffer styles handle changeable weather best.

## What Your Jacket Colour Says About Your Team or Brand

Colour is one of the most powerful tools in visual identity — and in group jackets, it communicates something before anyone reads a single word of your design. The colour you choose for your team or brand jacket sends a signal. Here's what the most popular choices communicate, and how to think about your selection.

## Black: Authority, Sophistication, Confidence

Black is the most versatile and perennially popular jacket colour. It communicates professionalism, confidence, and a premium feel. In streetwear, it reads as cool and restrained. In corporate settings, it reads as polished and serious. It's also the most practical choice if your team needs to wear the jacket in formal and informal settings alike.

The risk with black: it can look generic without strong design work. If you're going black, your embroidery, patches, and design details need to do the heavy lifting.

## Navy: Heritage, Trust, Tradition

Navy is the classic collegiate colour and communicates trust, reliability, and a certain understated credibility. It's not trying too hard — it just looks established. Navy is a natural choice for schools, rowing clubs, swimming teams, and any organisation that values a sense of tradition.

Navy also pairs beautifully with white, gold, or red — giving you strong secondary colour options for your design.

## Maroon and Burgundy: Warmth, Premium, Distinction

Maroon and burgundy communicate a sense of warmth, richness, and distinction. It's a colour that reads as premium without the coldness of black or the conservatism of navy. It's become increasingly popular for university sports teams, rugby clubs, and anyone who wants to stand out from the sea of navy and black while still looking serious.

## Red: Energy, Urgency, Passion

Red is a bold statement. It communicates energy, passion, and intensity — which is why it's dominant in high-energy sports like football and basketball. For brands, red signals confidence and assertiveness. It's hard to ignore in a crowd, which makes it excellent for teams that want to be seen.

Red needs to be used thoughtfully. With the wrong secondary colours, it can read as aggressive or chaotic rather than powerful.

## Green: Growth, Nature, Originality

Forest green has had a significant resurgence in popularity. It communicates a sense of groundedness, originality, and connection to nature — which is why it's popular with outdoor sports, environmental brands, and teams that want something distinctive without being jarring. Green paired with cream or gold creates a particularly premium, considered look.

## White and Cream: Clean, Minimal, Premium

White or cream jacket bodies communicate cleanliness, minimalism, and a quietly premium aesthetic. They're harder to maintain than darker colours, which means wearing one signals that you take care of things — a subtle message that works well for aspirational brands and prestige garments like graduation jackets.

## Choosing Your Colour

The right colour for your team is the one that honestly reflects who you are — not just what looks good in isolation. Think about how the jacket will be worn, where it will be seen, and what you want the people wearing it to feel.

## 7 Ways to Personalise a Varsity Jacket Beyond the Standard Letter

The chenille letter is the classic varsity jacket personalisation — and there's a reason it's stood the test of time. But if you want your jacket to stand out, or if you're designing for a brand rather than a traditional sports team, there's a whole range of customisation options that go well beyond the standard letter. Here are seven worth knowing about.

## 1. Embroidered Name on the Chest

Individual names embroidered on the chest — either the right or left side — are one of the most popular upgrades for group orders. It transforms a team jacket into a personal item that each member genuinely owns. Names can be in block text, script, or a custom font that matches your brand aesthetic.

## 2. Full-Back Embroidered Design

The back of a varsity jacket is prime real estate. A full-back design — whether it's a detailed crest, a large logo, a skyline, or an illustrated graphic — creates a statement piece rather than just a team jacket. For brands and creative projects, this is often where the design investment makes the biggest visual impact.

## 3. Sleeve Stripe Customisation

The stripes on varsity jacket sleeves are part of the classic design, but they don't have to be standard white. You can customise sleeve stripes in any colour, or even add additional bands in contrasting colours. For brand-aligned jackets, matching sleeve stripes to specific brand colours creates a polished, intentional look.

## 4. Chenille Patches (Beyond the Letter)

Chenille patches don't have to be letters. They can be numbers, symbols, mascots, logos, or abstract shapes. The texture and dimensionality of chenille creates a distinctive, premium look that flat embroidery can't replicate. Consider chenille for the main design element on the front chest or back.

## 5. Custom Lining

The interior lining of a varsity jacket is often overlooked as a design surface. A custom-printed or custom-coloured lining — visible when the jacket is open or the sleeves are pushed up — adds a layer of detail that's unexpected and memorable. Brands often use the lining to include additional branding, a pattern, or a message.

## 6. Pocket Embroidery

The hand pockets on a varsity jacket are another often-underused canvas. Small embroidered logos, symbols, or text on the pocket flap or inside the pocket welt can add detail without overwhelming the overall design.

## 7. Custom Labels and Neck Tags

This one goes beyond the visible surface of the jacket. Custom woven labels or neck tags with your brand name, logo, or a personal message make the jacket feel genuinely branded from the inside out. It's a small detail that makes a big difference to how the finished product feels as a branded item.

## Designing Your Custom Jacket

All of these personalisation options are available across a full custom varsity jacket range. Whether you want one personalisation or all seven, a good design team will help you put together something that looks intentional and premium.

content:
## Oversized vs Fitted: Which Jacket Silhouette Is Right for Your Team?

Jacket fit is one of those decisions that gets underestimated in group orders. Teams spend a lot of time choosing colours and customisation options, then rush the fit decision — and end up with jackets that look great on some people and awkward on others.

Here's an honest breakdown of oversized vs fitted silhouettes to help your team make the right call.

## The Case for Oversized Jackets

Oversized jackets — cut with extra room through the chest, shoulders, and length — are currently dominant in streetwear and youth fashion. The look is relaxed, comfortable, and distinctly modern. It works across a range of body types without the same sizing precision that a fitted jacket demands.

For groups, oversized is often actually easier to manage. Because the fit is intentionally loose, minor sizing differences matter less. A team where members range from a slim build to a more athletic frame can often order fewer size variations and still achieve a consistent, intentional look.

**Oversized works best for:** Streetwear brands, youth teams, music and creative communities, casual group orders where comfort matters as much as style.

## The Case for Fitted Jackets

A fitted jacket sits closer to the body — following the natural shape of the shoulders, chest, and waist rather than adding volume. Done well, a fitted jacket looks sharp, structured, and professional. It communicates effort and intentionality, which is why it's the preferred silhouette for corporate teams, event staff, and sports clubs that want a polished look.

The trade-off with fitted jackets is that sizing matters more. If you order a medium for someone who should be in a large, the difference is obvious in a way it wouldn't be with an oversized cut. This makes size collection more important — and returns or exchanges more likely if the sizing process was rushed.

**Fitted works best for:** Corporate teams, event staff, sports teams that train in a structured uniform, professional environments where the jacket represents the brand.

## What About Sizes Across a Mixed Team?

For most group orders, the realistic answer is that you're ordering for a team with a range of body types. Here's how to think about it:

If the jacket is intentionally oversized as a design choice, tell your team to order their regular size or size down. The oversized look will still come through, but they won't be swimming in the jacket.

If the jacket is fitted, encourage your team to measure carefully rather than guessing. For anyone who is between sizes, sizing up is usually the safer choice — a slightly large fitted jacket is more comfortable than one that restricts movement.

## Which Looks Better on Photos and Social Media?

Oversized jackets tend to photograph very well when styled intentionally — loose jeans, clean trainers, relaxed pose. Fitted jackets look excellent in team photos and professional settings, particularly when everyone is similarly built.

If your team is producing content and wants the jacket to appear in photos or videos, consider how the silhouette will read on camera. Both can look excellent — but they read very differently.

title: How Streetwear Brands Are Using Custom Varsity Jackets to Build Identity
excerpt: Custom varsity jackets have become a cornerstone of streetwear brand-building. Here's how independent labels and emerging brands are using them.
content:
## How Streetwear Brands Are Using Custom Varsity Jackets to Build Identity

In streetwear, the varsity jacket has undergone a full reinvention. What was once primarily a sports team staple is now one of the most strategic tools in a brand's visual identity toolkit. Independent labels, emerging designers, and even established streetwear houses are using custom varsity jackets not just as products — but as statements.

Here's what's driving the trend, and what it means if you're building a brand.

## The Varsity Jacket as a Walking Billboard

A custom varsity jacket worn in public is about as effective as advertising gets. It's worn at events, in cities, at universities, and shared across social media. Unlike a t-shirt that stays hidden under a coat, a jacket is visible, wearable, and memorable.

Streetwear brands understand this. A well-designed jacket with your logo, colourway, and patches is something people choose to wear again and again — not because they have to, but because it looks good and makes them feel part of something. That's the most powerful form of marketing there is.

## Limited Runs Create Exclusivity

Smart streetwear brands don't always order hundreds of units. Many place intentionally small runs — sometimes as few as 20-50 jackets — to create scarcity. When people know only a limited number exist, the jacket becomes a collectible, not just a garment.

This approach builds hype, drives demand, and creates a secondary market. It also reduces the financial risk of a large initial order — brands can test demand with a small run before scaling up.

## Customisation as Storytelling

The best custom varsity jackets tell a story. Patches, embroidered text, sleeve stripes in specific colours, chenille lettering — each element is chosen deliberately to communicate something about the brand's identity, values, or narrative.

A brand's first season might feature their launch year. Their anniversary edition might feature a number that references a founding date. Collaborations might incorporate two colour palettes or two sets of branding. Every design decision is a communication opportunity.

## Community Jackets vs. Merch Jackets

There are two different strategic uses of varsity jackets in streetwear. Community jackets are produced for the brand's inner circle — creative directors, collaborators, event staff, loyal early customers. They're not for sale and they signal belonging. These are the jackets that get photographed and shared, and they build credibility before the brand has mass reach.

Merch jackets, on the other hand, are sold to the public. These tend to be more accessible in price and design, allowing a wider audience to participate in the brand's world.

Both serve a purpose. Many brands use the community jacket strategy first to build credibility, then expand into commercial merch.

## What This Means for Your Brand

If you're building a brand — streetwear, music, creative, sport — a custom varsity jacket is worth considering as a brand asset rather than just merchandise. Think about what story you want to tell, who you want wearing the jacket, and how you want to release it.

## The Most Popular Varsity Jacket Colour Combinations Right Now

Choosing the right colour combination for your custom varsity jacket is one of the most impactful decisions you'll make. Get it right and the jacket looks sharp, cohesive, and intentional. Get it wrong and even a well-made jacket can look off.

This is the modern spin on the classic letterman. The high contrast between a matte black wool body and clean white sleeves is bold, clean, and contemporary. It's one of the most requested combinations for university groups, music acts, and fashion-forward sports teams.

Classic, heritage, and unmistakably collegiate. Navy and white is the combination most associated with the original American varsity jacket. It's timeless in the best way — it never looks dated, works with virtually any logo colour, and photographs exceptionally well.

Maroon (or burgundy) has seen a surge in popularity in recent years, particularly among rugby clubs, hockey teams, and university sports societies. Paired with white sleeves, it creates a warm, premium-looking jacket that reads as classic without being generic.

One of the biggest trends right now for streetwear and fashion-forward groups. Cream or off-white body with brown (tan) leather sleeves has a vintage, premium feel that's very different from the traditional collegiate look. It's bold but warm, and tends to be a conversation starter.

Many teams and brands order jackets that directly match their brand colour palette. If your team has established colours, use them — consistency across your uniforms, merchandise, and branding builds a stronger visual identity.

title: How to Order Custom Jackets for a Corporate Team Across Multiple Locations

content:
## How to Order Custom Jackets for a Corporate Team Across Multiple Locations

When your team is spread across multiple offices, sites, or cities, ordering custom jackets adds a logistical layer that most single-site teams don't have to deal with. Who collects sizes? Where do the jackets get delivered? How do you manage different delivery addresses without the order becoming a nightmare?

Here's a practical framework that makes multi-location jacket orders work.

## Start With a Central Point of Contact

Even if your team is spread across multiple locations, the order itself should be managed by one person or team. This central coordinator is responsible for collecting all the information (sizes, personalisation details, delivery addresses) and communicating with the supplier on behalf of the whole group.

Each location should have a local contact who is responsible for gathering sizes from their site and feeding them back to the central coordinator. This two-layer approach keeps communication manageable without putting all the burden on one person.

## Collect Sizes Location by Location

Rather than trying to collect sizes from everyone at once across all sites, break it down by location. Create a separate Google Form or spreadsheet tab for each site and assign each local contact responsibility for filling it in.

Set the same deadline for all locations. Once you have responses from each site, compile them into a single size list before submitting to the supplier.

## Decide on Delivery in Advance

Multi-location orders can be delivered in several ways: one central delivery point (and then distributed internally), individual delivery to each site, or a combination. Discuss this with your supplier early — some suppliers can handle split deliveries to multiple addresses at no extra charge, while others may add a fee for each additional delivery location.

If you're doing internal distribution from a central point, make sure you have a plan for how jackets get from the hub to individual team members at each site.

## Standardise the Design Across All Locations

For corporate orders, consistency is key. All jackets should look the same regardless of the wearer's location. The only variation should be individual personalisation (name, department, or location label if desired).

Agree on the final design once, get it approved centrally, and communicate it to local contacts as a finalised decision rather than seeking further feedback.

## Plan for Size Variations and Replacement Orders

In a multi-location order, the chance of someone receiving the wrong size or a jacket being lost in transit is higher than with a single-site delivery. Build in a small buffer of units (typically 3-5% extra) in the most common sizes to handle replacements.

Also confirm with your supplier how top-up or replacement orders work — can you reorder single units if needed? At what cost?

## What Information Do You Need Before Placing a Bulk Jacket Order?

If you've ever submitted a bulk jacket inquiry and received a vague reply, or waited days for a quote that still needed more information — the problem usually isn't the supplier. It's that the inquiry didn't include the details needed to price and plan the order accurately.

Coming prepared with the right information doesn't just speed things up. It also gives you more control over the process, helps you get accurate pricing on the first pass, and reduces the risk of surprises down the line.

Here's everything you need before you place your first inquiry.

## 1. Jacket Style and Type

What kind of jacket are you ordering? Varsity, bomber, puffer, fleece, coach? The style affects pricing, lead times, and customisation options. If you're not sure which style fits your needs, that's okay — but mention what you're trying to achieve so the supplier can make a recommendation.

## 2. Quantity

How many jackets do you need? Even a rough number is helpful at the inquiry stage. Most custom jacket suppliers price on volume — 10 jackets costs more per unit than 100. Knowing your quantity upfront ensures you get the right pricing bracket.

## 3. Size Breakdown

If you know it, include how many of each size you need. If you haven't collected sizes yet, you can indicate the total quantity and note that sizes are still being confirmed.

## 4. Colour Requirements

What colours do you want for the body, sleeves, lining, and any other panels? If you have brand colours with Pantone references or hex codes, include them. If you're working from a logo, share the file.

## 5. Customisation Details

What do you want printed or embroidered on the jackets? This includes: logo placement (left chest, back, sleeves), personalisation (individual names or numbers), additional text (team name, year, slogan), and decoration technique (embroidery, chenille, printed).

If you have artwork files ready, share them at the inquiry stage. Vector files (.ai, .eps) are ideal.

## 6. Deadline or Event Date

When do you need the jackets? Be specific — include the event or delivery date if there is one. Custom jackets typically take 3-6 weeks from design approval to delivery.

## 7. Budget Expectation

You don't have to share an exact figure, but having a rough per-unit budget in mind helps the supplier recommend the right product tier.

title: Group Jacket Orders: How to Manage Approvals, Sizes & Payments as a Team
excerpt: Running a group jacket order? Coordinating approvals, sizes, and payments across a team can quickly become overwhelming. Here's how to manage it smoothly.
content:
## Group Jacket Orders: How to Manage Approvals, Sizes & Payments as a Team

Placing a group jacket order sounds straightforward — until you're the one responsible for chasing 30 people for their sizes, getting everyone to agree on a design, and figuring out who owes what. It's one of those tasks that feels easy until you're in the middle of it.

Here's how to manage the three biggest challenges of group orders — design approvals, size collection, and payments — without losing your mind.

## Managing Design Approvals

Getting group consensus on a design is where most orders stall. The key is to limit the decision-makers early. If everyone gets a vote, you'll never reach agreement.

Instead, designate one or two people to make final design decisions. Get a design proof from your supplier, share it with the decision-makers only, and collect feedback in a single round. This is not the time for open-ended discussion threads.

Once the design is approved by the designated decision-makers, communicate the final version to the group as a done deal: 'Here's the final design — production starts next week.' This prevents late-stage requests for changes that delay the whole order.

## Collecting Sizes Efficiently

Use a Google Form. Seriously — it's the single most effective tool for this. Create a form with three questions: name, size preference, and any personalisation details. Share a size guide alongside it and ask people to measure themselves rather than guess from a previous garment — most sizing disputes come from guessing, not measuring.

Set a hard deadline, communicate it clearly, and don't extend it. Send one reminder 48 hours before the deadline and leave it there — over-messaging just trains people to ignore the reminders. Whoever hasn't responded by the deadline gets assigned a default size or is excluded from the initial order.

Plan for 10-15% non-response even with a good system, and do a final sanity check on the size spread before you submit — if you're seeing 30 larges and zero extra-larges, something's probably gone wrong and it's worth a second look before the order goes in.

## Managing Payments in a Group

Payment collection is where the most friction happens, especially when people are contributing different amounts or paying individually. Here are three approaches that work:

**Centralised payment:** One person (usually the organiser) pays upfront and is reimbursed by the team. This is the fastest approach but requires someone willing to carry the cost temporarily.

**Payment platform:** Tools like PayPal or GoCardless let you collect payments individually without handling cash. Set up a payment link for the per-unit cost and share it with the group.

**Club or organisation budget:** If you're ordering for a school, club, or company, check whether there's an existing budget or expense process you can use.

## Timeline: When to Do What

Design approval should happen first, before size collection. Once the design is locked, share the form for sizes. Give people 5-7 days to respond. Once sizes are collected, submit the order.

## A Final Word

The biggest group order problems all come from unclear communication and undefined deadlines. Be specific, be firm, and be the person who makes decisions rather than waiting for everyone to agree.
