## How to Write a Design Brief for Your Custom Jacket Order (With Examples)

One of the most common reasons custom jacket orders go wrong — or take longer than expected — is a vague design brief. When the supplier doesn't have a clear picture of what you want, they make assumptions. And those assumptions are often wrong.

A good design brief doesn't need to be complicated. It just needs to cover the right information clearly. Here's exactly what to include, with examples.

## What Is a Design Brief?

A design brief is a document (even a structured email or message works) that tells your custom jacket supplier exactly what you want. It's your chance to communicate colours, placement, text, logos, and any specific requirements before production begins.

## What to Include in Your Design Brief

**1. Jacket style and quantity** Start with the basics. What style of jacket are you ordering? How many units? What's the size breakdown? *Example: 25 x varsity jackets. Size breakdown: 3 S, 7 M, 8 L, 5 XL, 2 XXL.*

**2. Colour selection** Specify the body colour, sleeve colour, and lining colour. If you have Pantone references or hex codes, include them. *Example: Body — Navy (Pantone 289C). Sleeves — White faux leather. Lining — White.*

**3. Logo and artwork** Share your logo in the highest quality format you have — ideally vector (.ai or .eps). Specify where you want the logo placed. *Example: Main logo embroidered on left chest. Secondary text 'Class of 2026' on the back below the main design.*

**4. Personalisation requirements** Do individual jackets need names, numbers, or positions? If so, provide a list with each person's name and the text to be applied.

**5. Font preferences** If you have a preference for a specific font or style (block letters, script, varsity chenille), say so.

**6. Deadline** Always include when you need the jackets by. Be realistic — custom jackets typically take 3-6 weeks depending on complexity and order size.

**7. Budget expectation** You don't have to share an exact figure, but a rough per-unit budget helps your supplier recommend the right product tier.

## What Not to Do

Don't send a brief that just says 'like this photo' with a reference image. Reference images are helpful context, but they're not a replacement for written specs. Also, don't skip the size breakdown — this is the detail that holds up more orders than any other.

## How to Collect Sizes From Your Team Without the Back-and-Forth Headache

If you've ever tried to collect sizes from a group of people for a uniform or jacket order, you already know the pain. You send a message. Half the people ignore it. Some respond with 'I'm not sure, probably medium?' Three people give you the wrong size. And then someone changes their answer the day before the deadline.

It doesn't have to be this chaotic. Here's a system that actually works.

## Why Size Collection Goes Wrong

The problem usually isn't that your team is unhelpful — it's that the process is unclear. When people don't know exactly what information you need, or why it matters, they procrastinate or guess. The key is to make it as easy as possible to respond correctly the first time.

## Step 1: Send a Size Guide With Your Request

Never ask for a size without including a size guide. People don't always know their size — especially in a brand they haven't bought from before. Send a simple chest measurement guide or a link to the size chart, and ask them to measure themselves rather than guess from a previous garment.

## Step 2: Use a Simple Google Form or Shared Spreadsheet

The single biggest upgrade you can make to the process is moving away from asking via text, email, or group chat. Set up a Google Form with three fields: name, size, and any personalisation details. Share the link and set a clear deadline.

## Step 3: Set a Hard Deadline — and Stick to It

The deadline has to be real. Tell your team that any responses received after the deadline will default to a specific size, or simply won't be included in the order. This sounds firm, but it eliminates the endless chasing.

## Step 4: Account for No-Responses in Advance

Plan for 10-15% non-response, even with a perfect system. Decide in advance what your default size will be, or whether you'll exclude non-responders from the initial order and handle them separately as a top-up later.

## Step 5: Do a Final Count Before Submitting

Before you submit your order, do a quick sanity check. Is the size distribution realistic? If you have 30 larges, 2 smalls, and 0 extra-larges, something probably went wrong.

title: Genuine Leather vs Faux Leather Sleeves: What's the Real Difference?

## Genuine Leather vs Faux Leather Sleeves: What's the Difference?

When ordering a custom varsity jacket, the sleeve material affects the jacket's appearance, price, weight, and durability. The two most common options are genuine leather and faux leather.

### Genuine Leather Sleeves

Genuine leather is made from real animal hide, usually cowhide. It has a natural texture, premium feel, and strong durability. With proper care, genuine leather can last for many years and may develop a unique aged appearance over time.

Best for: premium varsity jackets, award and graduation jackets, small custom orders, customers who want long-lasting quality.

Main benefits: premium look and feel, strong and durable, holds its shape well, becomes more attractive with age.

The main disadvantages are the higher price, heavier weight, and need for regular care.

### Faux Leather Sleeves

Faux leather, also called PU leather or synthetic leather, is a man-made material designed to look like real leather. It is lighter, more affordable, easy to clean, and available in many colours.

Best for: bulk varsity jacket orders, schools, teams, and clubs, budget-conscious customers, customers who prefer animal-free materials.

Main benefits: more affordable, lightweight, easy to clean, consistent colour and texture, wide range of colours.

However, lower-quality faux leather may peel or crack after extended use and usually does not last as long as genuine leather.

### Which Option Should You Choose?

Choose genuine leather when you want a premium, durable jacket that can last for years. Choose faux leather when you need an affordable, lightweight, and consistent option for a larger group order.

## Best Jackets for School Uniforms: What to Look for Before You Order

If you're coordinating jackets for a school — team spirit wear, a graduating class, or a full uniform programme — the choice you make affects how it looks, how long it lasts, and how much back-and-forth you deal with during ordering. Here's what actually matters.

## Durability Comes First

School jackets get worn hard: hallways, sports practice, being stuffed in lockers, washed repeatedly. Look for reinforced seams at the shoulders and sleeve joins, quality snap buttons or zips, and a fabric that holds its shape after regular washing. Melton wool and cotton twill both hold up well to this kind of everyday use.

## The Right Style for Your School

A varsity jacket is the traditional choice for school spirit and sports teams — instantly recognisable, and built around chenille letters, names, and years. A bomber jacket offers a more modern, lightweight option that still takes embroidery well for smaller school crests or logos. Fleece hoodies work as a softer, casual alternative for everyday wear rather than a formal team identity piece.

## Consistent Sizing Across a Big Order

The bigger the order, the more sizing matters. Share a size guide with every student or parent before collecting measurements — this single step prevents most of the exchange requests that come from guessed sizes rather than measured ones.

## Customisation That Represents the School Properly

School jackets should carry the school name, crest, or mascot clearly, and the decoration method matters. Chenille reads as the classic letterman choice; embroidery is cleaner for smaller detail and text.

## Bomber vs Varsity vs Puffer: Which Jacket Should You Buy in 2025?

Looking to buy a new jacket but unsure which style suits you best? With so many options available, choosing between a bomber, varsity, and puffer jacket can be confusing. Each style offers unique advantages and works best for different occasions, climates, and personal preferences.

In this comprehensive guide, we'll break down the key differences between these three popular jacket styles and help you make an informed decision.

## Bomber Jackets: The Modern Essential

Bomber jackets have evolved significantly since their military aviation roots. Originally designed for pilots in World War II, modern bombers are now a streetwear staple.

**Key characteristics:** fitted, tapered silhouette; ribbed cuffs and hem; short length (hits right around the waist); lightweight to mid-weight options; perfect for both casual and semi-formal settings.

Best for: bombers work best in mild to moderate weather and pair excellently with jeans, chinos, or dress pants.

## Varsity Jackets: Timeless Team Spirit

Varsity jackets, also called letterman jackets, combine wool bodies with leather sleeves for a classic athletic aesthetic. They're perfect for school pride, team uniforms, or retro-inspired fashion.

**Key characteristics:** large wool body with leather sleeves; button or snap closures; endless potential for custom patches and personalization; heavier weight material; iconic college and high school aesthetic.

Best for: varsity jackets are ideal for cooler climates and casual wear. They offer excellent customization potential for teams and organizations.

## Puffer Jackets: Maximum Warmth and Comfort

Puffer jackets are engineered for serious cold-weather protection using down or synthetic insulation.

**Key characteristics:** heavily insulated with down or synthetic fill; distinct quilted pattern design; bulkier, cozy silhouette; water-resistant options available; available in various lengths.

Best for: puffers are best for winter climates and outdoor activities where staying warm is your top priority.

## How to Choose: Quick Decision Guide

Choose a bomber jacket if you live in a mild climate, want versatile everyday styling options, prefer a fitted modern look, or need a clean piece perfect for layering.

Choose a varsity jacket if you want a classic, timeless style, are looking for heavy customization options, are part of a school, team, or organization, or prefer a bold statement piece.

Choose a puffer jacket if you live in a genuinely cold climate, warmth is your number one priority, you want a water-resistant option for snow or rain, or you spend a lot of time outdoors in the winter.

## Final Thoughts

The best jacket depends entirely on your climate, lifestyle, and personal style preferences. Many people invest in multiple styles to cover different seasons and occasions. Whatever you choose, make sure it fits well and reflects your personal style.

## What Does a Custom Jacket Cost? Pricing Guide for Schools, Teams and Brands

The cost of a custom jacket depends on its style, materials, design details, and order quantity. A simple bulk jacket will cost less than a premium varsity jacket with genuine leather sleeves and multiple chenille patches.

### What Affects Custom Jacket Pricing?

#### Jacket Style

Varsity jackets usually cost more because they require heavier materials and more detailed construction. Bomber, coach, fleece, and lightweight jackets are often more affordable.

#### Materials

Premium materials such as Melton wool, genuine leather, and quilted lining increase the price. Twill bodies, polyester fabrics, and faux leather sleeves provide a more budget-friendly alternative.

#### Customisation

The number and type of decorations also affect the final cost. Options may include: embroidered logos, chenille patches, tackle-twill lettering, individual names and numbers, custom labels, printed lining, sleeve and back designs. Simple designs are generally more affordable than jackets with several large patches and personalised details.

#### Order Quantity

The more jackets you order, the lower the cost per unit will usually be. Individual jackets have a higher production cost, while schools, teams, and brands can benefit from bulk pricing.

### Estimated Custom Jacket Prices

General price ranges may include: individual orders approximately $120–$200 or more per jacket; small group orders approximately $75–$120 per jacket; medium bulk orders approximately $60–$90 per jacket; large wholesale orders approximately $45–$70 per jacket. These are only estimates.

### Pricing by Jacket Type

**Varsity jackets** are a premium option for schools, sports teams, clubs, and graduation groups. Wool bodies, leather sleeves, chenille patches, and knitted ribbing can increase the cost.

**Bomber jackets** offer a modern appearance at a mid-range price. They are popular for corporate teams, event staff, and branded merchandise.

**Coach jackets** are lightweight, practical, and affordable. They are a strong choice for events, staff uniforms, and larger budget-conscious orders.

**Puffer jackets and fleece hoodies** — puffer jackets provide greater warmth but may cost more because of their insulated construction. Fleece hoodies are generally more affordable and work well for everyday winter teamwear.

### How to Reduce the Cost

You can keep your order within budget by ordering a larger quantity, using fewer patches or logos, choosing faux leather instead of genuine leather, selecting twill instead of wool, avoiding urgent production, and finalising all sizes and artwork before production.

### Request an Exact Quote

Every custom jacket order is different. For accurate pricing, share your preferred jacket style, quantity, materials, design, sizes, and delivery country.

## Three ways letterman jackets get decorated

Letterman jackets tell a story through patches: sports letters, positions, years, mascots, and sponsor marks. The three most common decoration families are chenille, direct embroidery, and tackle twill appliqué.

## Chenille: bold, plush, and classic

Chenille uses yarn tufted into felt bases for a plush, retro look. It reads from a distance and is synonymous with traditional varsity awards. Because it is thick, designers usually limit how many oversized chenille pieces compete on one panel.

## Direct embroidery: detail and corporate marks

Direct embroidery stitches thread into the garment for fine detail, small text, and corporate logos. It is flatter than chenille and ideal for chest logos, sleeve hits, and name bars that need crisp edges.

## Tackle twill: big shapes with clean edges

Tackle twill cuts fabric letters or shapes, edges them with zig-zag or satin stitch, and sews them to the jacket. It splits the difference between bold shape and flatter profile, common for numbers and large name arcs.

## Durability and where you place each method

Durability depends on stitch quality and how often the jacket is dry-cleaned or spot-cleaned. Chenille can snag if caught on sharp equipment; embroidery can abrade if constantly rubbed by backpack straps—placement matters.

## Build a clear visual hierarchy

When mixing methods, hierarchy helps: one hero back patch, medium chenille initials on the front, and embroidery for fine copy. That layout photographs cleanly and avoids a cluttered silhouette.

## Next steps

Choosing thread colors, felt bases, and upload formats is easiest once you've settled on a method mix for your design.

## What defines a bomber jacket

The bomber jacket (often traced to military flight jackets like the MA-1) is a waist-length zippered jacket with elastic or knit ribbing at the cuffs, hem, and collar. It is meant to seal in warmth while staying easy to move in, which is why it became a civilian staple for pilots, motorcyclists, and later streetwear.

## Materials and linings you will see today

Classic bombers use nylon shell, leather, suede, or satin, sometimes with a bright contrast lining in orange or safety tones on vintage military styles. Modern fashion bombers simplify lining color but keep the compact silhouette.

## Bomber vs varsity: how the styles differ

Compared to a varsity or letterman jacket, a bomber is usually zip-front only, with less contrast color blocking on the body, and without the traditional wool body / leather sleeve combination—though fashion houses often blur the lines.

Varsity jackets emphasize school or team storytelling: chenille letters, large back patches, striped ribs, and a snap front. Bombers skew cleaner—better for minimalist logos, small chest embroidery, or tonal debossed leather.

## Fit, uniforms, and which silhouette to pick

Fit-wise, bombers often sit at high hip with enough room across the shoulders for layering a hoodie. Varsity jackets can run slightly boxier to accommodate patch layouts and a heavier wool face.

For corporate uniforms or staff drops, a neutral bomber in black, navy, or olive takes embroidery well without overwhelming a small logo. For spirit wear and senior class identity, a varsity profile still carries more tradition.

## Custom bombers

Custom bombers are available across leather, suede, nylon, satin, and softshell-type builds so you can match the jacket type to the story you want to tell—not just the trend cycle.

## Why letterman jackets need special care

A custom letterman or varsity jacket combines wool or wool-blend body fabric, leather or faux-leather sleeves, knit ribbing at the cuffs and hem, and chenille or embroidered patches. Each material reacts differently to water, heat, and friction, so a gentle routine protects your investment.

## Before you clean

Read the manufacturer care label inside the jacket. Test any cleaner on a hidden area (inside hem or pocket bag) first. Work on a clean, flat surface with light-colored towels underneath.

When in doubt, spot-clean only and avoid machine washing finished jackets with leather sleeves or heavy chenille, because agitation can shrink wool, crack coatings, and lift patch edges.

## Wool body: brushing and spot treatment

For the wool body, use a soft clothes brush after wear to remove dust. Treat small stains with a slightly damp microfiber cloth and a tiny amount of wool-safe detergent, blotting from the outside of the stain inward. Never scrub in circles, which can fuzz the melton surface.

## Leather and faux-leather sleeves

Leather and high-quality faux-leather sleeves should be wiped with a dry or barely damp cloth. If the sleeve picks up salt or sweat marks, use a cleaner formulated specifically for that material, applied to the cloth first—not directly on the jacket.

## Patches, ribs, drying, and storage

Chenille letters and large tackle-twill patches are stitched through the body lining. Avoid soaking those areas. If a thread loosens, stop pulling and have it reinforced so the patch does not ripple.

Rib knit cuffs, collar, and waistband can hold body oils. A short steam session from a handheld steamer (without pressing the iron plate onto the rib) refreshes the fibers. Keep the steamer head moving so you do not overheat elastic content.

Air-dry the jacket on a wide, padded hanger in a ventilated room. Never tumble dry. When you are not wearing it, store it in a breathable garment bag away from direct sunlight so colors stay true.

## When to call a professional

If your jacket has a wool and leather build, keep an eye on both fabrics separately since they age differently. If you need a deep clean or restoration, use a specialist cleaner experienced with award jackets.
